```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(ggplot2)
```

*Getting started* (`vignette("fmriAR-introduction")`) ran the default
workflow on noise that matched its assumptions. This vignette covers the
choices behind it: why to pass the design to `fit_noise()`, how the AR order
is chosen and how to tell when it is too low, when an ARMA model fits better,
standard errors that tolerate leftover autocorrelation, and filters specified
in AFNI's restricted form.

The examples use the same kind of simulated study as *Getting started*: two
runs of 150 volumes at a TR of 2 seconds, an event-related task, an intercept
for each run and a set of cosine drift terms per run. Only the noise changes
from section to section.

```{r helpers}
library(fmriAR)
set.seed(7)

TR <- 2
n_per_run <- 150
runs <- rep(1:2, each = n_per_run)
n_time <- length(runs)

hrf <- function(t) dgamma(t, 6) - dgamma(t, 16) / 6
h <- hrf(seq(0, 30, by = TR))
event_regressor <- function(n) {
  onsets <- cumsum(sample(6:10, n, replace = TRUE))
  stim <- tabulate(onsets[onsets <= n], nbins = n)
  x <- stats::filter(stim, h / max(h), sides = 1)
  as.numeric(replace(x, is.na(x), 0))
}
cosines <- function(n, k) {
  sapply(seq_len(k), function(j) cos(pi * j * (seq_len(n) - 0.5) / n))
}

# Task, one intercept per run, and k cosine drift terms per run
make_design <- function(k = 3) {
  X <- cbind(task = c(event_regressor(n_per_run), event_regressor(n_per_run)),
             run1 = runs == 1, run2 = runs == 2)
  if (k > 0) {
    none <- matrix(0, n_per_run, k)
    X <- cbind(X, rbind(cosines(n_per_run, k), none),
                  rbind(none, cosines(n_per_run, k)))
  }
  X
}

# Noise for n_vox voxels, each run simulated separately: an AR process with
# coefficients `ar`, plus optional white noise with standard deviation white_sd
simulate_noise <- function(n_vox, ar, white_sd = 0) {
  one_run <- function() {
    as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = ar), n = n_per_run)) +
      rnorm(n_per_run, sd = white_sd)
  }
  replicate(n_vox, c(one_run(), one_run()))
}
```

```{r acf-helpers, include = FALSE}
# Summaries and plot for the per-voxel autocorrelation check
acf_summary <- function(resid, stage, max_lag = 8) {
  a <- acorr_diagnostics(resid, runs = runs, max_lag = max_lag,
                         aggregate = "none")
  data.frame(stage = stage, lag = a$lags, ci = a$ci,
             lo = apply(a$acf, 1, quantile, 0.025),
             mid = apply(a$acf, 1, median),
             hi = apply(a$acf, 1, quantile, 0.975))
}
whitened_resid <- function(plan, X, Y) {
  w <- whiten_apply(plan, X, Y, runs = runs)
  w$Y - w$X %*% qr.coef(qr(w$X), w$Y)
}
plot_acf_check <- function(acs, good) {
  acs$status <- ifelse(acs$stage %in% good, "Whitened", "OLS")
  ci <- acs$ci[1]
  ggplot(acs, aes(lag)) +
    annotate("rect", xmin = -Inf, xmax = Inf, ymin = -ci, ymax = ci,
             fill = "grey88") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = 0.3, colour = "grey55") +
    geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi, colour = status), linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_point(aes(y = mid, colour = status), size = 1.7) +
    facet_wrap(~stage, nrow = 1) +
    albersdown::scale_color_albers(limits = c("Whitened", "OLS"), guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(1, 4, 8)) +
    labs(x = "Lag (volumes)", y = "Autocorrelation") +
    theme(strip.background = element_blank(),
          strip.text = element_text(hjust = 0),
          panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
}
```

## Why `design = X` matters

The noise model is estimated from residuals, and residuals are not the noise.
Fitting a model removes from the data whatever the regressors can
reproduce, and that includes some of the noise. In matrix terms the residuals
are $My$, where $M = I - X(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top$ is the projection that
removes the design, so their covariance is $M \Sigma M$ rather than the
noise covariance $\Sigma$.

The effect is a downward bias in the estimated autocorrelation, and drift
regressors cause most of it: slow cosines soak up slow fluctuations, which is
where autocorrelated noise keeps its power. The figure below fits an AR(1)
model to the same noise, coefficient 0.5, under designs with more and more
drift terms.

```{r bias}
noise <- simulate_noise(2000, ar = 0.5)

n_drift <- c(0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12)
bias <- t(sapply(n_drift, function(k) {
  X_k <- make_design(k)
  r <- lm.fit(X_k, noise)$residuals
  c(drift_terms = k,
    plain = fit_noise(r, runs = runs, p = 1)$phi[[1]],
    corrected = fit_noise(r, runs = runs, p = 1, design = X_k)$phi[[1]])
}))
round(bias, 3)
```

```{r fig-bias, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Estimated AR(1) coefficient as drift terms are added to the design. The noise is the same throughout and its true coefficient is 0.5 (grey line). Without the design, the estimate falls steadily; with design = X it stays at the truth."}
bd <- data.frame(k = rep(bias[, "drift_terms"], 2),
                 phi = c(bias[, "plain"], bias[, "corrected"]),
                 fit = rep(c("OLS", "Whitened"), each = nrow(bias)))
ends <- bd[bd$k == max(bd$k), ]
ends$txt <- ifelse(ends$fit == "OLS", "without design", "design = X")
ggplot(bd, aes(k, phi, colour = fit)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linewidth = 0.4, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.8) +
  geom_text(data = ends, aes(label = txt), hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.4,
            size = 3.1, colour = "grey25") +
  annotate("text", x = max(n_drift) + 0.4, y = 0.5, label = "truth", hjust = 0,
           size = 3.1, colour = "grey45") +
  albersdown::scale_color_albers(limits = c("Whitened", "OLS"), guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = n_drift, expand = expansion(add = c(0.5, 3))) +
  labs(x = "Cosine drift terms per run", y = "Estimated coefficient") +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
```

`design = X` undoes the projection: `fit_noise()` works out the bias that
$M$ puts into each lag of the autocovariance and inverts it. It works with
every pooling mode for AR models, and with censoring. It needs residuals that
really are OLS residuals from `X`; a numerical check rejects obvious
mismatches. At 12 drift terms per run the corrected estimate starts to slip,
because so few degrees of freedom remain per run; that many drift terms is
unusual.

Two helpers expose the same correction. `noise_acvf(resid, design = X)`
returns the corrected autocovariance itself. `acvf_bias_matrix()` builds the
correction once, to pass to `fit_noise(acvf_correction = )` for many
datasets that share the same design, run structure and censored frames.

## Choosing the AR order

With `p = "auto"` (the default) `fit_noise()` tries every order from 0 to
`p_max` (default 6) and keeps the one with the lowest BIC. Pooling many
voxels gives BIC more evidence than one series would, but neighbouring voxels
share fluctuations, so `fit_noise()` counts them at an effective number:
$V / (1 + (V - 1)\bar r)$ for $V$ voxels with mean inter-voxel correlation
$\bar r$. That is a deliberately conservative count.

The design correction matters here too. Projection bias distorts every lag a
little, and with thousands of voxels BIC treats those small, systematic
distortions as structure worth extra coefficients. Here the noise is AR(2):

```{r order}
X <- make_design(3)
noise_ar2 <- simulate_noise(2000, ar = c(0.4, 0.2))
r_ar2 <- lm.fit(X, noise_ar2)$residuals

c(without_design = fit_noise(r_ar2, runs = runs)$order[["p"]],
  with_design    = fit_noise(r_ar2, runs = runs, design = X)$order[["p"]])
```

Without the design, the search adds four coefficients that describe the
projection, not the noise.

### What an order that is too low looks like

The check from *Getting started* is how you find out whether an order is too
low. Below, the same AR(2) noise is whitened with an AR(1) model and with the
AR(2) model the search chose. The AR(1) filter removes most of the lag-1
autocorrelation but leaves the voxels outside the white-noise band at lags 1
and 2.

```{r underfit}
plan_ar1 <- fit_noise(r_ar2, runs = runs, p = 1, design = X)
plan_ar2 <- fit_noise(r_ar2, runs = runs, design = X)
```

```{r fig-underfit, echo = FALSE, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "The whiteness check for AR(2) noise. Lines span the middle 95% of voxels; dots mark the median; the grey band is where 95% of one voxel's values fall if its noise is white. An AR(1) filter fails the check at lags 1 and 2; the AR(2) filter passes it."}
acs <- rbind(acf_summary(r_ar2, "OLS"),
             acf_summary(whitened_resid(plan_ar1, X, noise_ar2), "AR(1)"),
             acf_summary(whitened_resid(plan_ar2, X, noise_ar2), "AR(2)"))
acs$stage <- factor(acs$stage, levels = c("OLS", "AR(1)", "AR(2)"))
plot_acf_check(acs, good = "AR(2)")
```

## Robust standard errors

When some autocorrelation survives whitening, the ordinary standard error is
off again, in a direction that depends on what was missed.
`sandwich_from_whitened_resid()` offers `type = "hac"`, a Newey–West
estimator computed within runs, which allows for leftover autocorrelation at
short lags. `type = "hc0"` allows for unequal variances only.

Applied to the AR(2) noise above, every voxel is a null voxel, so the share
passing $|t| > 1.96$ should be 5%:

```{r robust}
false_positive_rate <- function(plan, type) {
  w <- whiten_apply(plan, X, noise_ar2, runs = runs)
  fit <- lm.fit(w$X, w$Y)
  se <- sandwich_from_whitened_resid(w$X, w$Y, beta = fit$coefficients,
                                     type = type, runs = runs)$se
  mean(abs(fit$coefficients["task", ] / se[1, ]) > 1.96)
}
rates <- sapply(c("iid", "hac"), function(type) {
  c(`AR(1), too low` = false_positive_rate(plan_ar1, type),
    `AR(2), correct` = false_positive_rate(plan_ar2, type))
})
knitr::kable(rates, digits = 3,
             caption = "Share of null voxels with |t| > 1.96, by noise model and standard error.")
```

With the under-fitted model the ordinary standard error is wrong; here it
errs on the cautious side, and in other cases it errs the other way. HAC
brings the rate back toward 5%. With the right model the two agree. Use HAC
as a safety net when a model cannot pass the check above, not as a substitute
for a good noise model. HAC standard errors have no small-sample correction,
so in short runs they are approximate.

## ARMA models

Scanner noise adds white noise on top of the autocorrelated physiological
noise. An AR(1) process plus white noise is no longer AR(1): it is
ARMA(1,1), with one autoregressive and one moving-average coefficient. A pure
AR model can mimic it only with extra coefficients.

```{r arma}
noise_mix <- simulate_noise(2000, ar = 0.8, white_sd = 1)
r_mix <- lm.fit(X, noise_mix)$residuals

plan_ar_auto <- fit_noise(r_mix, runs = runs, design = X)
plan_arma <- fit_noise(r_mix, runs = runs, method = "arma", p = 1, q = 1)

plan_ar_auto$order
plan_arma
```

ARMA models are estimated by the Hannan–Rissanen procedure, pooled over
voxels: each voxel is a replicate series sharing the coefficients, and no lag
crosses a run boundary or a censored frame. `hr_iter` adds refinement
iterations.

The BIC search picked AR(`r plan_ar_auto$order[["p"]]`). ARMA(1,1) does the
same job with two coefficients. Both pass the whiteness check at lags 1 to 3
(about 5% of voxels outside the band is what white noise gives) and both give
valid tests:

```{r arma-compare}
score <- function(plan) {
  rw <- whitened_resid(plan, X, noise_mix)
  a <- acorr_diagnostics(rw, runs = runs, max_lag = 3, aggregate = "none")
  w <- whiten_apply(plan, X, noise_mix, runs = runs)
  fit <- lm.fit(w$X, w$Y)
  se <- sandwich_from_whitened_resid(w$X, w$Y, beta = fit$coefficients)$se
  c(rowMeans(abs(a$acf) > a$ci),
    mean(abs(fit$coefficients["task", ] / se[1, ]) > 1.96))
}
plan_ar1_mix <- fit_noise(r_mix, runs = runs, p = 1, design = X)
tab <- rbind(`AR(1)` = score(plan_ar1_mix),
             `AR, order by BIC` = score(plan_ar_auto),
             `ARMA(1,1)` = score(plan_arma))
colnames(tab) <- c("outside, lag 1", "lag 2", "lag 3", "false positive")
knitr::kable(tab, digits = 3,
             caption = "Share of voxels outside the white-noise band, and false-positive rate, for AR(1) plus white noise.")
```

`method = "arma"` also accepts `p = "auto"` and `q = "auto"`, searching
`0:p_max` and `0:q_max` by BIC. Pooling thousands of independent voxels gives
that search a great deal of evidence, and it tends to choose the largest
orders on offer. When theory suggests an order, as here, set it; otherwise
check what the search returns.

## AFNI-style restricted filters

AFNI describes some noise models by their roots rather than their
coefficients: an AR(3) with one real root `a` and one complex pair (radius
`r1`, angle `t1`), or an AR(5) with a second pair (`r2`, `t2`), plus an
optional share of white noise. `afni_restricted_plan()` turns such a
specification into an ordinary plan that `whiten_apply()` can use. It does
not estimate the roots; you supply them, for example to match a simulation
set up in AFNI's `1dgenARMA11`.

```{r afni}
roots <- list(a = 0.5, r1 = 0.4, t1 = pi / 3)
plan_afni <- afni_restricted_plan(r_ar2, runs = runs, p = 3L, roots = roots,
                                  estimate_ma1 = FALSE)
round(plan_afni$phi[[1]], 3)
```

`a`, `r1` and `r2` must be non-negative; values above 0.95 are clamped to
0.95 and angles are clamped to $[0, \pi]$. The additive white noise is set
by `vrt`, the share of variance carried by the AR part. With `vrt` below 1
and `estimate_ma1 = FALSE`, the plan is the exact ARMA(p, p) equivalent of
AR(p) plus white noise: its autocorrelation is `vrt` times the AR
autocorrelation at every nonzero lag.

```{r afni-vrt}
plan_afni_vrt <- afni_restricted_plan(r_ar2, runs = runs, p = 3L,
                                      roots = c(roots, vrt = 0.8),
                                      estimate_ma1 = FALSE)
plan_afni_vrt$order
```

With `estimate_ma1 = TRUE` (the default) the roots fix the AR part, an MA(1)
term is estimated from the AR-filtered residuals, and `vrt` is ignored.
`parcels` and a list of root specifications keyed by parcel ID give each
parcel its own filter. `compat$afni_restricted_plan()` is the same function
under the compatibility interface.
